title: What Does "Eternal" Mean?
hook: Does eternal punishment really mean punishment that never ends?
tldr: Hebrew olam and Greek aion/aionios mean an age or a long but often finite period, not timeless endlessness. Latin translation and Augustine's Neoplatonism turned them into eternity. Kolasis means corrective pruning. So Matthew 25:46's kolasin aionion is better read as an age of corrective punishment.
big_idea: Eternal punishment means an age of correction, not endless torture.

points.title: The Bible has no word for eternity
points.text: Scholars from Ellicott to Campbell Morgan agree: neither Old Testament Hebrew nor New Testament Greek has a word for abstract, timeless eternity. Reading it in is an anachronism.

points.title: Olam means an age
points.text: Olam describes Jonah's three days in the fish, Babylon's seventy-year ruin, the showbread covenant now ended, and an earth to be replaced. Long, but finite.

points.title: Aionios means pertaining to an age
points.text: Aion, the Greek for olam, means an age with a beginning and end. Romans speaks of a mystery hidden for aionios ages, now revealed: not eternally hidden.

points.title: Augustine and the Vulgate added infinity
points.text: Jerome's Vulgate rendered aionios as aeternum, and Neoplatonist Augustine argued God's eternity makes punishment eternal, confusing God's timelessness with finite human sin.

points.title: Aidios was available but not used
points.text: Aidios, the closest Greek word to unending, appears only twice, for God's power and angels' chains held until judgment day. It is never used for hell.

points.title: Kolasis is pruning
points.text: Kolasis originally meant pruning a plant to correct its growth. Plato and Aristotle used it for remedial punishment for the offender's good, unlike vengeful retribution.

sections.h: Justice, consequences and the question of duration
sections.summary: Justice demands punishment; otherwise murder and theft go unchecked, bringing chaos. Retribution deters and protects society. The opposite extreme from ECT hellfire expects no afterlife punishment at all, but the gravity of some actions implies unavoidable consequences. What measures will be taken, and against whom, may be unknowable. If there is a period of correction, we must ask its nature, intent and duration; this topic focuses on duration.

Reading an ancient Near Eastern Jewish text with Western eyes risks the anachronism fallacy. Eternity as debated in Western philosophy essentially does not exist in the biblical context. Baptists, Calvinists, fundamentalist evangelicals, Pentecostals and other conservative Protestant and Catholic groups have long taught endless abusive torment. But the Greek and Hebrew words translated eternal or everlasting carry nuances that, properly understood, challenge hell as endless punishment.

sections.h: Scholars: the Bible has no word for eternity
sections.summary: Interpreter's Dictionary of the Bible: neither Testament knows eternity as timelessness; aion meant vital force, life, then age, lifetime. Charles Ellicott on Matthew 25:46: aionios means duration through an age or ages, applied to periods with beginning and end. Hasting's Dictionary: no Hebrew or Greek word for abstract eternity. Encyclopedic Dictionary: olam means an indefinitely long period, of old, not from eternity. Weymouth: aeonion means belonging to the ages, not during.

Herman Oldhausen: the Bible has no expression for endlessness; its terms denote long periods. Knappe of Halle: Hebrew lacked any single word for endless duration, and pure eternity appears in no ancient language. Charles H. Welch of The Berean Expositor: eternity is not a biblical theme and lies outside revelation's scope. G. Campbell Morgan, conservative pastor and Cheshunt College president: there is no word in the whole Bible corresponding with our eternal.

Olam, often rendered forever or eternal, generally means an age or agelong: long, not necessarily infinite. Even in modern Hebrew, an olam imprisonment, a life sentence, lasts 25 years, or 17 with good behavior. Jonah says the earth barred him in forever, yet he was in the fish three days and nights. Isaiah's palaces are lairs forever only until the Spirit is poured out and the wilderness becomes fruitful.

The showbread set out every Sabbath was a covenant forever, yet the practice ended when the Mosaic Law was fulfilled and replaced by the New Covenant. Ecclesiastes says the earth remains forever, yet a new heaven and earth will replace it. Jeremiah calls the land an everlasting ruin under Nebuchadnezzar, a desolation explicitly limited to seventy years.

Daniel 7:18 says the holy ones possess the kingdom forever, forever and ever, repeating the Aramaic equivalent of olam three times: for an age, and another age, and another age. The triple repetition may hyperbolically express going on and on, a perpetual succession of ages approaching eternity. This could be the only place in Scripture where eternity itself is referenced.

Olam, sometimes mistakenly translated forever, everlasting or eternal, more accurately means an age or a long but finite period. The biblical examples show durations that are significant and enduring but limited. Recognizing this is essential to interpreting divine promises and judgments, especially regarding hell, where eternal may have been misapplied, obscuring the true nature of God's judgment, justice and mercy.

Aion and aionios translate olam in the Septuagint and the New Testament. Aion means an age with a beginning and end; aionios means pertaining to an age. Strong's: a space of time, an age, a cycle. HELPS: an era characterized by a specific quality. Romans 16:25-26 speaks of a mystery hidden for aionios ages, kept for ages, not eternally. Endlessness is an exception set by context: Ephesians 3:21's to the ages of the ages may approach eternity.

Translations of aion and aionios often reflect translators' theology more than the words' meaning, shaping how we view God's character. Under Roman philosophical influence, Jerome's 4th-century Latin Vulgate often rendered aionios as aeternum, implying an unending state and shaping Western thought. Scholars debate rendering these words eternal; Young's Literal Translation and the Concordant Literal Translation use age-during or eon, suggesting eternal punishment is not inherent in the original texts.

sections.h: Augustine of Hippo: Neoplatonism and two fallacies
sections.summary: Platonic and Neoplatonic thought saw time as degraded eternity, adding infinity to aion. Neoplatonist Augustine argued that since God is eternal, His punishments must be timeless and unending. This is equivocation, conflating God's timeless existence with finite human sins so finite acts get infinite punishment, defying proportional justice and making God infinitely vengeful. It is also false analogy: eternal attributes need not be expressed eternally. And aionios in Matthew 25:46 depends on its subject.

sections.h: How the doctrine spread and was challenged
sections.summary: Augustine's view was not universal: Eastern Orthodoxy rejected it, focusing on judgment's purifying side. In the Middle Ages Aquinas systematized it, and the church used fear of damnation in sermons and art for moral manipulation and herd control. Luther and Calvin attacked fear tactics and indulgences but kept hellfire. Modern translations correct aionios: Young's age-during, Rotherham's age-abiding, the Concordant's eonian.

One reading: aidios is the Koine word closest to endless, possibly truly everlasting; had the New Testament meant hell was eternal, it would likely have used aidios, and it did not. A second reading: aidios means unbroken, enduring, unrelenting, and appears only twice: God's power, which nothing can limit, and the fallen angels' chains, held until the judgment of the great day. A chain lasting until a set day is bounded, not endless.

Kolasis, translated punishment, originally meant chastisement and correction, and in horticulture pruning: cutting parts of a plant to keep it healthy and productive. Plato used it for punishment that reforms the offender; in Gorgias he contrasts remedial kolasis with timoria, retribution satisfying the punisher's anger. Aristotle said kolasis serves the one punished. It was temporary and corrective, aiming at restoration. In 1 John 4:18 fear involves kolasis. Jesus may mean an age of corrective punishment.

Augustine's reading of aionios as eternal shaped Catholic and Protestant thought for centuries, yet his lack of proficiency in Greek produced lasting misunderstandings. Many English versions render kolasin aionion eternal punishment, while literal translations like Young's, the Concordant, Weymouth and Yale's The New Testament: A Translation give an agelong chastisement or the discipline of that age. Inconsistently translating aionios as forever here and age-lasting there confuses readers and distorts conclusions about divine judgment.

mythfact.fact: Its duration depends on what it modifies. Romans 16:25-26 speaks of a mystery hidden for aionios ages that was then revealed.

mythfact.myth: Forever in the Old Testament means without end.
mythfact.fact: Olam describes Jonah's three days in the fish and a seventy-year desolation: long, intense, but finite periods.

mythfact.myth: If eternal life is endless, eternal punishment must be too.
mythfact.fact: Aionios takes its duration from its subject: the life of the age to come versus corrective measures within a defined period.
Kolasis meant pruning and correction; Plato and Aristotle used it for remedial punishment that serves the one punished.

terms.meaning: Injecting modern ideas, like Western philosophical eternity, into an ancient text.
Hebrew for an age or agelong: a long, indefinite period, not necessarily infinite.
Greek for an age, and pertaining to an age; the equivalents of olam.
Greek for unbroken or enduring; closest to endless, used twice in the New Testament, never for hell.
Greek for corrective punishment; originally the pruning of plants to correct their growth.
Augustine's error of conflating God's timeless existence with the finite nature of human sins.

quiz.q: How long was Jonah's forever, olam, in the fish?
quiz.why: Jonah 1:17 says three days and nights; olam described an experience that felt endless but was limited.

quiz.q: What did kolasis originally mean in horticulture?
options: Pruning a plant to correct its growth
quiz.why: Pruning cuts parts of a plant to keep it healthy; likewise kolasis is corrective punishment aimed at restoration.

quiz.q: Which translation first rendered aionios with the Latin aeternum?
quiz.why: The 4th-century Vulgate's aeternum implied an unending state and shaped Western Christian thought on eternity.

reflect: How would your picture of God change if eternal punishment meant an age of correction rather than endless torment?
